subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the temperature of a substance?
items.correct: A measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles
items.misconception: The form of energy that flows from a hot object to a cold one
items.why: Everyday language uses 'heat' to mean hotness ('turn up the heat', 'feel the heat'), and both words are used in the same situations long before a particle model is taught. The fusion of heat with temperature is one of the most widely reported findings of research on students' thermal concepts. Keep the two apart. Temperature describes the state of a substance: how fast, on average, its particles move. Heat describes a process: energy passing from a hotter region to a colder one. Energy is transferred as heat; temperature is not transferred at all.
items.specStatementText: Chemical reactions involve a transfer of energy between the system and the surroundings, while total energy is conserved.
items.random_wrong: A measure of the total kinetic energy of all the particles it has

items.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid in an insulated cup, and the temperature of the solution rises. Which statement correctly describes the energy changes?
items.correct: The energy of the reacting chemicals falls by exactly the same amount as the energy of the surroundings rises.
items.misconception: Energy is created by the reaction, so the total energy of the system and the surroundings increases.
items.why: Everyday language describes energy as made and consumed: power stations 'produce' energy, fuels and batteries are 'used up'. Students carry this language into chemistry, where the energy is only transferred. Energy is conserved in every reaction. An exothermic reaction transfers energy from the chemicals to the surroundings; an endothermic reaction transfers energy from the surroundings to the chemicals. Nothing is created or destroyed.
items.specStatementText: Chemical reactions involve a transfer of energy between the system and the surroundings, while total energy is conserved.
items.random_wrong: The reacting chemicals gain energy, and the rise in the temperature of the solution shows this.

items.q: Solid ammonium nitrate is dissolved in water in a polystyrene cup, and the temperature of the water falls from 21.0 °C to 15.5 °C. Which statement explains the fall in temperature?
items.correct: Energy is transferred from the water to the dissolving solid, so the process is endothermic.
items.misconception: The solution is the system; it loses energy, so its temperature falls and the process is exothermic.
items.why: The reactants are dissolved in the water, so the mixture is seen as a single object whose temperature is 'the reaction's' temperature. Chemistry-education research on calorimetry reports that students frequently cannot say which part of a reaction mixture is the system and which the surroundings. Separate the two. The system is the reacting chemicals; the water around them is part of the surroundings, and the thermometer is in the water. An exothermic reaction transfers energy from the system to the water, so the water's temperature rises; an endothermic reaction takes energy from the water, so its temperature falls.
items.specStatementText: Reactions are described as endothermic or exothermic, depending on the direction of energy transfer between the system and the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: Cold is released by the dissolving solid and spreads out through all of the water in the polystyrene cup.

items.q: A student records observations for four reactions. Which reaction is endothermic?
items.correct: NaHCO₃(s) added to citric acid solution: the temperature falls by 4.5 °C
items.misconception: Fe(s) and S(s) heated briefly: the glow continues after the heating stops
items.why: Endothermic reactions are taught as 'taking in heat', and holding a reaction mixture in a Bunsen flame looks like giving it heat. The belief that exothermic reactions need no energy input is widely reported in chemistry-education research. Distinguish the energy needed to start a reaction (the activation energy, which both kinds of reaction have) from the energy transferred overall (ΔH). An exothermic reaction may need a spark or brief heating to start, and an endothermic reaction may start on its own at room temperature.
items.specStatementText: Reactions are described as endothermic or exothermic, depending on the direction of energy transfer between the system and the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: Mg(s) added to dilute HCl(aq): the temperature rises by 11.5 °C

items.q: The energy profile of an endothermic reaction is sketched with reaction coordinate on the x-axis and potential energy on the y-axis. Which statement about this profile is correct?
items.correct: The products are at a higher potential energy than the reactants.
items.misconception: The products are more stable than the reactants, as they have more energy.
items.why: In everyday use, having more energy means being stronger or more robust, and students are often told that chemicals 'store' energy, which makes a high-energy substance sound substantial rather than unstable. Stability is judged by potential energy: lower is more stable. A system that can lose energy by changing into something else is less stable than the substance it would become.
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of reactants and products determines whether reactions are endothermic or exothermic.
items.random_wrong: It shows an energy barrier, which the profile of an exothermic reaction lacks.

items.q: An energy profile for a reaction is plotted with reaction coordinate on the x-axis and potential energy on the y-axis. Relative to the same zero, the reactants are at 150 kJ mol⁻¹, the top of the energy barrier is at 280 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products are at 40 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for the reaction?
items.correct: −110 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: +110 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
Students take the point of view of the surroundings (or of the person observing), who gain energy in an exothermic reaction, and 'giving out' energy sounds like a positive amount. Sign errors of this kind are widely reported in chemistry-education research on thermochemistry. ΔH is the change in the system: final minus initial. If the system ends with less energy than it started with (exothermic), ΔH is negative; if it ends with more (endothermic), ΔH is positive.

Working: ΔH = potential energy of products − potential energy of reactants = 40 kJ mol⁻¹ − 150 kJ mol⁻¹ = −110 kJ mol⁻¹. (The barrier height above the reactants, 280 − 150 = 130 kJ mol⁻¹, is the activation energy and does not enter ΔH.)
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of reactants and products determines whether reactions are endothermic or exothermic.
items.working: ΔH = potential energy of products − potential energy of reactants = 40 kJ mol⁻¹ − 150 kJ mol⁻¹ = −110 kJ mol⁻¹. (The barrier height above the reactants, 280 − 150 = 130 kJ mol⁻¹, is the activation energy and does not enter ΔH.)

items.q: For the reaction P → Q, where P and Q are two substances, ΔH = −60 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement about the reaction is correct?
items.correct: P has more potential energy than Q, so Q is the more stable of the two substances.
items.misconception: P has the greater potential energy, so it is the more stable of the two.
items.why: In everyday use, having more energy means being stronger or more robust, and students are often told that chemicals 'store' energy, which makes a high-energy substance sound substantial rather than unstable. Stability is judged by potential energy: lower is more stable. A system that can lose energy by changing into something else is less stable than the substance it would become.
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of reactants and products determines whether reactions are endothermic or exothermic.
items.random_wrong: Q has more potential energy than P, so P is the more stable substance.

items.q: A spirit burner containing ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is used to heat 150.0 g of water in a copper can. Burning 0.920 g of ethanol raises the temperature of the water from 19.0 °C to 40.5 °C. Use c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and A_r values H 1.01, C 12.01, O 16.00. What value of ΔH for the combustion of ethanol do these results give?
items.correct: −6.75 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: −6.75 × 10⁵ kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
c is given in J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ but ΔH is always quoted in kJ mol⁻¹, and the change of unit is easily overlooked in a multi-step calculation. Unit errors of this kind are routinely reported in calorimetry calculations. Track the units at each step: J from Q = mcΔT, then ÷ 1000 for kJ, then ÷ n for kJ mol⁻¹. An answer a thousand times larger than typical enthalpy changes (tens to thousands of kJ mol⁻¹) signals a missing conversion.

Working: ΔT = 40.5 °C − 19.0 °C = 21.5 °C = 21.5 K. Q = mcΔT = 150.0 g × 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 21.5 K = 13 480.5 J = 13.48 kJ. M(C₂H₅OH) = 2(12.01) + 6(1.01) + 16.00 = 46.08 g mol⁻¹; n = 0.920 g / 46.08 g mol⁻¹ = 0.019965 mol. ΔH = −Q/n = −13.48 kJ / 0.019965 mol = −675 kJ mol⁻¹ = −6.75 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹ (3 s.f.).
items.specStatementText: The standard enthalpy change for a chemical reaction, ΔH⦵, refers to the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions and states. It can be determined from the change in temperature of a pure substance.

items.q:
50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is placed in a polystyrene cup and 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) is added. The temperature of the mixture rises by 4.50 °C.
HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)
Assume that the solutions have a density of 1.00 g cm⁻³ and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is ΔH for the reaction?
items.correct: −56.4 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: −28.2 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
In many calorimetry calculations only one reactant is quantified, so students do not learn to ask which reactant limits the reaction; the first-named or larger amount is then chosen by default. Find the amount of each reactant, use the equation's mole ratio to identify the one that is used up, and divide Q by the amount of that limiting reactant.

Working: m(solution) = (50.0 + 25.0) cm³ × 1.00 g cm⁻³ = 75.0 g. Q = mcΔT = 75.0 g × 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 4.50 K = 1410.75 J = 1.411 kJ. n(HCl) = 0.0500 dm³ × 1.00 mol dm⁻³ = 0.0500 mol; n(NaOH) = 0.0250 dm³ × 1.00 mol dm⁻³ = 0.0250 mol. The mole ratio is 1:1, so NaOH is limiting and 0.0250 mol of reaction occurs. ΔH = −Q/n = −1.411 kJ / 0.0250 mol = −56.4 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: The standard enthalpy change for a chemical reaction, ΔH⦵, refers to the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions and states. It can be determined from the change in temperature of a pure substance.
items.working: m(solution) = (50.0 + 25.0) cm³ × 1.00 g cm⁻³ = 75.0 g. Q = mcΔT = 75.0 g × 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 4.50 K = 1410.75 J = 1.411 kJ. n(HCl) = 0.0500 dm³ × 1.00 mol dm⁻³ = 0.0500 mol; n(NaOH) = 0.0250 dm³ × 1.00 mol dm⁻³ = 0.0250 mol. The mole ratio is 1:1, so NaOH is limiting and 0.0250 mol of reaction occurs. ΔH = −Q/n = −1.411 kJ / 0.0250 mol = −56.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: 4.00 g of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, is dissolved in 50.0 g of water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature of the water falls from 21.60 °C to 15.40 °C. Assume that all the energy absorbed comes from the water, c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, and that no energy is exchanged with the air. A_r values: H 1.01, N 14.01, O 16.00. What is ΔH for dissolving ammonium nitrate?
items.correct: +25.9 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: −25.9 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
Q = mcΔT gives a positive number for a temperature rise and a negative number for a fall, and it seems natural that 'more heat' is a positive enthalpy change. The minus sign in ΔH = −Q/n looks like a formality and is dropped. Q is the energy gained by the surroundings; ΔH is the energy change of the system. They always have opposite signs, which is what the minus sign expresses.

Working: ΔT = 15.40 °C − 21.60 °C = −6.20 K. Q = mcΔT = 50.0 g × 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ × (−6.20 K) = −1295.8 J = −1.296 kJ (energy gained by the water is negative: the water lost energy). M(NH₄NO₃) = 2(14.01) + 4(1.01) + 3(16.00) = 80.06 g mol⁻¹; n = 4.00 g / 80.06 g mol⁻¹ = 0.04996 mol. ΔH = −Q/n = −(−1.296 kJ) / 0.04996 mol = +25.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: The standard enthalpy change for a chemical reaction, ΔH⦵, refers to the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions and states. It can be determined from the change in temperature of a pure substance.
items.working: ΔT = 15.40 °C − 21.60 °C = −6.20 K. Q = mcΔT = 50.0 g × 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ × (−6.20 K) = −1295.8 J = −1.296 kJ (energy gained by the water is negative: the water lost energy). M(NH₄NO₃) = 2(14.01) + 4(1.01) + 3(16.00) = 80.06 g mol⁻¹; n = 4.00 g / 80.06 g mol⁻¹ = 0.04996 mol. ΔH = −Q/n = −(−1.296 kJ) / 0.04996 mol = +25.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Which statement about the standard enthalpy change of a reaction, ΔH⦵, is correct?
items.correct: It is the heat transferred at constant pressure with every substance in its standard state.
items.misconception: Its value is the same whether a product such as water forms as a liquid or as a gas.
items.why: State symbols are often treated as optional decoration on equations, and omitting them is a routine comment in examiner reports; students do not connect them with the energy change of melting or boiling. Always read and write state symbols. Condensing a gas releases energy, so forming H₂O(l) is more exothermic than forming H₂O(g); a ΔH⦵ value applies only to the states shown.
items.specStatementText: The standard enthalpy change for a chemical reaction, ΔH⦵, refers to the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions and states. It can be determined from the change in temperature of a pure substance.
items.random_wrong: It is the total heat transferred in an experiment, whatever amount of each reactant is used.

items.q: The graph shows the energy profile of a reaction. What is ΔH for the reverse reaction, in which the products are converted back into the reactants?
items.correct: −100 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: +150 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
Both quantities are drawn as vertical arrows starting from the reactants' level on the same diagram, and both are described as 'the energy of the reaction'. Confusing the two when reading energy profiles is widely reported. Measure ΔH from the reactants' level to the products' level; measure Ea from the reactants' level to the top of the barrier. The barrier height affects how easily the reaction starts, not the overall energy change.

Working: For the reverse reaction the start is the product level (150 kJ mol⁻¹) and the end is the reactant level (50 kJ mol⁻¹): ΔH = 50 − 150 = −100 kJ mol⁻¹, equal in size and opposite in sign to ΔH(forward) = +100 kJ mol⁻¹. The peak at 300 kJ mol⁻¹ does not enter ΔH.
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of reactants and products determines whether reactions are endothermic or exothermic.
items.working: For the reverse reaction the start is the product level (150 kJ mol⁻¹) and the end is the reactant level (50 kJ mol⁻¹): ΔH = 50 − 150 = −100 kJ mol⁻¹, equal in size and opposite in sign to ΔH(forward) = +100 kJ mol⁻¹. The peak at 300 kJ mol⁻¹ does not enter ΔH.

items.q: The diagram shows the energy profile of a reaction, with four vertical arrows labelled W, X, Y and Z. Which arrow represents the enthalpy change, ΔH, of the reaction?
items.correct: Arrow Y
items.misconception: Arrow X
items.why: Students focus on the downhill part of the curve, where energy is released, and do not subtract the energy taken in on the uphill part. Follow the whole path: up by Ea, then down to the products. The net change is products minus reactants, which is ΔH; the heights of the barrier cancel out.
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of reactants and products determines whether reactions are endothermic or exothermic.

items.q: A student adds 4.50 g of ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl(s), to 50.0 g of water in a polystyrene cup at 2 min and records the temperature every minute. The graph shows the readings, with the warming line extrapolated back to the time the solid was added. c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; A_r values: H 1.01, N 14.01, Cl 35.45. Assume that all the energy absorbed comes from the water. What value for the enthalpy change of solution of NH₄Cl do these results give?
items.correct: +13.7 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: +12.4 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
In earlier courses the maximum (or minimum) temperature is simply read from the thermometer, and the reason for extrapolating is not appreciated: energy is already being exchanged with the surroundings while the mixture is still warming or cooling, so the recorded extreme underestimates the change. Examiner reports repeatedly note candidates taking the highest recorded temperature instead of the extrapolated value. Plot temperature against time, draw the best straight line through the readings after the reaction, and extend it back to the time of mixing. The temperature change is the difference between the initial temperature and this extrapolated value, which is larger than the difference to the recorded maximum (or minimum).

Working: From the graph, the initial temperature is 22.0 °C and the warming line extrapolated back to 2 min gives 16.5 °C, so ΔT = 22.0 − 16.5 = 5.5 K (the recorded minimum, 17.0 °C, is not used because the solution was already gaining energy from the air). Q = mcΔT = 50.0 g × 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 5.5 K = 1149.5 J = 1.1495 kJ. The water is the surroundings and loses this energy, so for the surroundings Q = −1.1495 kJ. M(NH₄Cl) = 14.01 + 4(1.01) + 35.45 = 53.50 g mol⁻¹; n = 4.50 g / 53.50 g mol⁻¹ = 0.08411 mol. ΔH = −Q/n = −(−1.1495 kJ) / 0.08411 mol = +13.7 kJ mol⁻¹ (endothermic, positive).
items.specStatementText: The standard enthalpy change for a chemical reaction, ΔH⦵, refers to the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions and states. It can be determined from the change in temperature of a pure substance.
items.working: From the graph, the initial temperature is 22.0 °C and the warming line extrapolated back to 2 min gives 16.5 °C, so ΔT = 22.0 − 16.5 = 5.5 K (the recorded minimum, 17.0 °C, is not used because the solution was already gaining energy from the air). items.q: The energy profiles shown are drawn to the same scale for two reactions of the same reactant A: in reaction 1, A forms product B, and in reaction 2, A forms product C. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Product B is more stable than product C.
items.misconception: Reaction 2 takes less time than reaction 1.
items.why: Most graphs that students meet in science have time on the x-axis, and labels such as 'progress of reaction' sound like time. Labelling the x-axis 'time' is a common error in students' sketches of energy profiles. Label the x-axis 'reaction coordinate' and read it as progress along the reaction pathway. How fast a reaction goes is a separate question, answered by rate measurements, not by the length of the x-axis.
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of reactants and products determines whether reactions are endothermic or exothermic.
items.random_wrong: Product C is more stable than reactant A.

items.q: A student mixes 25.0 cm³ of 1.20 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) with 25.0 cm³ of 1.20 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) in a polystyrene cup at 3.0 min and records the temperature every minute, as shown in the graph. Which temperature change, ΔT, should the student use in Q = mcΔT?
items.why:
The word 'final' is read literally as 'last reading'. Students do not separate the temperature change caused by the reaction from the later, slower change caused by the mixture returning towards room temperature. The temperature change caused by the reaction is complete by the time the extrapolated line starts; everything after that is energy exchange with the room. Use the extrapolated maximum (or minimum), not the last reading.

Working: The mixture starts at 20.0 °C. After the highest reading (27.0 °C at 5 min) the temperature falls along a straight line because energy is lost to the surroundings; this cooling was already happening while the mixture was warming. Extrapolating the cooling line back to the moment of mixing, 3.0 min, gives 28.0 °C, the temperature the mixture would have reached with no energy loss. ΔT = 28.0 − 20.0 = 8.0 °C = 8.0 K (a temperature difference has the same value in °C and K).
items.specStatementText: The standard enthalpy change for a chemical reaction, ΔH⦵, refers to the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions and states. It can be determined from the change in temperature of a pure substance.

items.q: Is a large beaker of water at 60 °C at a higher temperature than a small beaker of water at 60 °C?
items.correct: No. Both are at 60 °C, because the average kinetic energy of the particles is the same. The larger sample has more particles, so it would transfer more heat to its surroundings as it cooled.
items.misconception: Temperature depends on the amount of substance: a larger sample contains more energy, so it has 'more temperature'.
items.why: Students generalize from quantities that do add up, such as mass, volume and energy, and from experience that a large pan of hot water warms a room more than a cup does. Predicting that two cups of water at 50 °C mixed together will be at 100 °C is a documented response in thermal-concept research. Temperature is an average over the particles, so it does not depend on how many there are. The total energy transferred on heating or cooling does depend on the amount, which is why Q = mcΔT contains the mass.
items.specStatementText: Chemical reactions involve a transfer of energy between the system and the surroundings, while total energy is conserved.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When water is boiling and energy is still being supplied, does its temperature rise?
items.correct: No. At the boiling point the energy supplied is used to overcome the attractions between the particles, not to increase their average kinetic energy, so the temperature stays constant until all the water has boiled.
items.misconception: Whenever heat is transferred to a substance its temperature must rise.
items.why: In most everyday heating the temperature does rise, so 'being heated' and 'getting hotter' come to mean the same thing. It is another form of treating heat and temperature as one quantity. Heat transferred to a substance can raise its temperature, but during a change of state it changes the arrangement of the particles instead and the temperature stays constant. Heat and temperature change are related through c and m only when no change of state occurs.
items.specStatementText: Chemical reactions involve a transfer of energy between the system and the surroundings, while total energy is conserved.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When ammonium nitrate dissolves in water and the water becomes colder, does 'cold' pass from the solid into the water?
items.correct: No. There is no substance or form of energy called 'cold'. Energy is transferred from the water to the dissolving substance, so the temperature of the water falls.
items.misconception: Cold is something that can be released or passed on, so an endothermic process gives out cold.
items.why: Everyday language treats cold as an entity ('shut the door, you're letting the cold in', 'ice gives off cold'), and research on students' thermal concepts reports explanations in terms of cold flowing. Only energy is transferred. An object or solution becomes colder because energy leaves it; in an endothermic process the energy leaves the water and enters the system.
items.specStatementText: Reactions are described as endothermic or exothermic, depending on the direction of energy transfer between the system and the surroundings.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In Q = mcΔT for a calorimetry experiment, what is m?
items.correct: The mass of the substance whose temperature change was measured: the water, or the whole of the solution (all the solutions mixed together). It is not the mass of a reactant, a fuel or just one of the solutions.
items.misconception: m is the mass of the substance that reacts: the solid dissolved, the fuel burned, or one of the reactant solutions.
items.why: Students link 'the energy of the reaction' to 'the mass of what reacts', and the reactant's mass is often the most prominent number in the question. Using the mass of the fuel or of the solid instead of the mass of water is a frequently reported error in calorimetry calculations. In mixing experiments the same error appears as using only the volume of the solution already in the cup, forgetting that the solution added is also warmed or cooled. Q = mcΔT describes the pure substance whose temperature was measured. Use the mass of the water or of the whole solution in the calorimeter; the reactant appears later, in n.
items.specStatementText: The standard enthalpy change for a chemical reaction, ΔH⦵, refers to the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions and states. It can be determined from the change in temperature of a pure substance.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the heat Q measured in a calorimetry experiment the same as ΔH?
items.correct: No. Q is the energy transferred for the amount that reacted in that experiment. ΔH is per mole of reaction: ΔH = −Q/n, in kJ mol⁻¹.
items.misconception: The heat measured in the experiment, given a positive or negative sign, is the enthalpy change; there is no need to divide by the amount that reacted.
items.why: Q and ΔH are both described as 'the energy of the reaction', and students do not attach the 'per mole' in the unit to what ΔH means. ΔH must not depend on how much was used in the experiment, so the heat measured is divided by the amount (mol) that reacted. The unit kJ mol⁻¹ is a reminder of this step.
items.specStatementText: The standard enthalpy change for a chemical reaction, ΔH⦵, refers to the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions and states. It can be determined from the change in temperature of a pure substance.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must a temperature change in °C be converted to kelvin by adding 273 before it is used in Q = mcΔT?
items.correct: No. A kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size, so a temperature change has the same value in both: a rise of 21.5 °C is a rise of 21.5 K. Adding 273 is correct for converting a temperature, not a temperature change.
items.misconception: Because c is in J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, ΔT must be converted to kelvin by adding 273.
items.why: Students learn the rule 'add 273 to convert to kelvin' for temperatures and apply it to every quantity measured in °C, including a difference between two temperatures. Convert temperatures, not changes. If both temperatures are converted, (T₂ + 273) − (T₁ + 273) = T₂ − T₁, so ΔT is the same in K and °C.
items.specStatementText: The standard enthalpy change for a chemical reaction, ΔH⦵, refers to the heat transferred at constant pressure under standard conditions and states. It can be determined from the change in temperature of a pure substance.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: On an energy profile, which distance represents the energy released by an exothermic reaction?
items.correct: The vertical distance between the reactant level and the product level, ΔH. Only the difference in potential energy between reactants and products is transferred to the surroundings.
items.misconception: The energy released by an exothermic reaction is the energy that was stored in the reactants, so on the profile it is the whole potential energy of the reactants, measured from the axis.
items.why: Everyday and earlier-course language: 'fuels store energy' and 'energy is stored in the bonds and released when they break'. Students then read the height of the reactants above the axis as the amount of energy available to be given out. The absolute potential energy of the reactants has no physical meaning on its own; the axis zero is arbitrary. The energy transferred to the surroundings is the drop from the reactant level to the product level, ΔH, because the products still hold the rest of the potential energy.
items.specStatementText: The relative stability of reactants and products determines whether reactions are endothermic or exothermic.
